findings.title: Unbounded slice allocation from an attacker-controlled deepObject array index in query-parameter decoding
findings.evidence: Source: the raw query string. urlValuesDecoder.DecodeObject, style "deepObject" (req_resp_decoder.go:660-681) extracts every bracketed segment of each query key with the regexp `\[(.*?)\]` and joins them into a nested props key. makeObject (:912-934) deepSets those into a nested map, then buildResObj (:970-995) hits the `array` branch and calls sliceMapToSlice(t). sliceMapToSlice (:938-960) does: `key, err := strconv.Atoi(k)` over the map keys, `max := -1; for _, k := range keys { if k > max { max = k } }`, then `for i := 0; i <= max; i++ { result = append(result, nil) }`. The only validation on the index is that it parses as an integer; nothing compares it against a configured maximum, the number of keys actually present, or any value the caller controls. buildResObj then does `resultArr := make([]any, len(arr))` and loops `for i := range arr` calling buildResObj once per slot, so the cost is paid twice - once in memory, once in CPU. The repository's own test suite proves the path is reachable from a query string: openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder_test.go:936-938 declares `Style: "deepObject"` with `objectOf("items", integerArraySchema)` and drives it with `query: "param[items][1]=456&param[items][0]=123"`. Substituting `param[items][2000000000]=1` walks the identical path with max = 2000000000, committing roughly 2e9 * 16 bytes of slice backing array before any schema rule is evaluated. A grep for bounds over the whole file (`max|Max|limit|Limit|bound`) returns only this local `max` variable and unrelated delimiter constants.
findings.impact: A single unauthenticated HTTP request with a short query string (a few dozen bytes) forces the validating process to allocate a slice sized by an integer the client chose, and then to iterate it. The result is memory exhaustion and process termination (Go runtime out-of-memory is not recoverable by the handler), or sustained CPU burn at lower indexes. Because openapi3filter is designed to run as request-validation middleware in front of the application (see openapi3filter/middleware.go), the crash takes the whole server down, not one handler. Repeated cheap requests give a reliable denial of service.
findings.preconditions: The served OpenAPI document declares a query parameter with `style: deepObject` whose object schema contains an array-typed property (directly, nested, or via additionalProperties). This is an ordinary, spec-conformant OpenAPI 3 declaration, not a debug or non-default setting of the library. The request must reach ValidateParameter: either the operation has no security requirement, or the deployment validates parameters before/alongside authentication (openapi3filter.Options.MultiError continues past a failed security check, validate_request.go:50-83).
findings.recommendation: Bound the reconstructed array by something the client does not choose, before allocating. In sliceMapToSlice, reject an index that exceeds the number of keys actually present (a dense array of n elements cannot have a maximum index above n-1), or compare it against a configurable ceiling exposed on openapi3filter.Options with a conservative default, and return a ParseError of Kind KindInvalidFormat when it is exceeded. Applying the check to `max` before the `for i := 0; i <= max; i++` loop and before `make([]any, len(arr))` in buildResObj closes both the allocation and the iteration. Rejecting negative indexes at the same point is worth doing while the guard is being written.
findings.limits: No runtime reproduction was executed: no Go toolchain is installed on this host (`go` is not on PATH), so the chain was established by reading it end to end rather than by running it. The finding does not establish what a specific deployment's spec declares; it establishes that the library allocates without a bound whenever a spec-conformant deepObject array parameter is declared. The exact index at which a given process dies depends on its memory limit.
findings.unaided_label: unbounded slice allocation from attacker-controlled deepObject array index

findings.title: Unchecked type assertion in deepSet panics on colliding deepObject query keys

location.component: deepSet, called from makeObject during deepObject query-parameter decoding

findings.evidence: deepSet (req_resp_decoder.go:899-908) walks a key path and creates intermediate maps: `if _, ok := m[key]; !ok { m[key] = make(map[string]any) }` followed by the unchecked `m = m[key].(map[string]any)` on line 905. The guard only creates a map when the key is ABSENT; when the key is present and holds a string, the assertion is executed against a string. makeObject (:911-933) feeds it from `for kk, value := range props` - a Go map, whose iteration order is randomized per range. The deepObject props builder (:660-681) derives those keys from the query string: `param[a]` yields matches `[a]` and the props key "a"; `param[a][b]` yields `[a]`,`[b]` and the props key "a\x1Fb". A request carrying both, e.g. `?param[a]=x&param[a][b]=y`, therefore produces two entries whose deepSet order decides the outcome. If "a" is processed first, mobj["a"] holds the string "x"; the subsequent deepSet(mobj, ["a","b"], "y") finds the key present, skips the map creation, and line 905 panics with `interface conversion: interface {} is string, not map[string]interface {}`. Nothing between the query string and line 905 rejects the collision: `strings.Contains(value, urlDecoderDelimiter)` on line 916 inspects the VALUE, not the key path, and the deepObject regexp accepts any bracket depth. The odds are per-pair, so an attacker who repeats the pattern with N independent prefixes (`?p[a]=1&p[a][z]=1&p[b]=1&p[b][z]=1&...`) drives the probability of at least one bad ordering to 1-2^-N; a couple of dozen pairs makes it effectively certain per request. The test suite exercises deepObject nesting heavily (req_resp_decoder_test.go:894-1120) but every case uses disjoint sibling keys - `param[obj][prop1]=bar&param[obj][prop2][badindex]=bad` at :1000 is the closest, and prop1/prop2 do not collide - so no test covers a prefix that is both a leaf and a branch.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated client controls whether a panic occurs inside the request-validation path. Under the shipped middleware (openapi3filter/middleware.go:119-138, which calls ValidateRequest from an http.Handler) net/http recovers the panic per connection: the client's connection is dropped with no response and a full goroutine stack trace is written to the server's error log, so a cheap request loop yields connection churn and unbounded log growth. Where a consumer calls ValidateRequest outside net/http's recovery - its own goroutine, a worker pool, a CLI, or a non-net/http transport - the panic is unrecovered and terminates the process.
findings.preconditions: The served OpenAPI document declares a query parameter with `style: deepObject` and an object schema (the only combination that reaches urlValuesDecoder.DecodeObject's deepObject branch). No array property and no authentication are required. Reachable through the request-body path too when a form-urlencoded property carries a deepObject encoding (UrlencodedBodyDecoder -> decodeProperty -> decodeValue -> DecodeObject).
findings.recommendation: Replace the unchecked assertion on line 905 with a checked one and turn the failure into a ParseError rather than a panic: `next, ok := m[key].(map[string]any); if !ok { return an error }`. deepSet must return an error and makeObject must propagate it, so a query key that is simultaneously a leaf and a branch is rejected as malformed input with a 400 instead of aborting the goroutine. The sibling helper deepGet (:886-897) already handles the same shape safely with a checked assertion, which is the pattern to copy.

triage.reason: Considered because net/http recovers handler panics, which could bound the impact to the attacker's own request. It does not reduce this to informational: the recovery is a property of one deployment shape, the stack trace still reaches the logs on every attempt, and openapi3filter is a library whose entry points (ValidateRequest, ValidateParameter) are exported and called from contexts net/http does not wrap.

findings.limits: No runtime reproduction was executed: no Go toolchain is on this host, so the panic was established by reading the assertion and the two call sites that can produce a colliding key path. The finding does not establish which consumers call ValidateRequest outside a recovering HTTP server; it establishes that the library panics rather than returning an error. The exact probability per request depends on Go's map iteration randomization, which is why the finding is stated in terms of repeated prefixes rather than a single deterministic payload.
findings.unaided_label: unchecked map type assertion in deepSet panics on colliding deepObject keys

findings.title: CI executes third-party code from mutable references, including an unversioned go install
findings.evidence: Nothing under .github/workflows is pinned by commit SHA. .github/workflows/go.yml uses actions/setup-go@v6, actions/cache@v3 and actions/checkout@v6; .github/workflows/shellcheck.yml uses actions/checkout@v2 and ludeeus/action-shellcheck@1.1.0. A git tag is a movable pointer, so none of these references is immutable. Beyond the actions, three steps fetch and execute Go modules resolved at run time: `go run golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/modernize/cmd/modernize@latest` and `go run golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/nilness/cmd/nilness@latest` in build-and-test, and - the sharpest of the three - `go install github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/v3@latest` in check-goimports, which then runs over every .go file in the checked-out tree (`find . -type f -iname '*.go' ... -exec goimports-reviser {} \;`). `@latest` carries no version at all, so the build has no record of what it executed. Both workflows trigger on `push` as well as `pull_request`, so these steps also run on the default branch, where the runner's credentials are not the reduced fork token. Pinned by 40-character SHA: 0 of 6 action references.
findings.impact: Anyone who gains control of one of these upstream references - a repointed tag, a compromised maintainer account, a hijacked module path - executes their code inside this repository's CI, with the workspace checked out and the runner's GITHUB_TOKEN in the environment. The goimports-reviser step is the widest: it is an individual-maintainer module, resolved at `@latest`, invoked with write access to every source file in the tree, so a malicious release could alter the source that the same run then tests and reports green.
findings.preconditions: Requires a third party to be compromised; nothing in this repository is exploitable on its own. This is why the finding is hardening rather than a claimed exploit path.
findings.recommendation: Pin every `uses:` to a 40-character commit SHA with the human-readable tag in a trailing comment, and let Dependabot or Renovate move the SHAs. Replace the three `@latest` module references with explicit versions - ideally a `tools.go` plus the go.sum the repository already maintains, so the toolchain is covered by `go mod verify`, which the workflow already runs for the library's own dependencies but not for the tools it executes.

triage.reason: The references cross an ownership boundary: ludeeus/action-shellcheck and github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser belong to individual third parties, and actions/* and golang.org/x/tools belong to GitHub and the Go team, none of them the getkin organisation. The same-owner exculpation in INF-16 does not apply to any of the six.

This is defence in depth, not a load-bearing control that is absent: exploitation requires an upstream compromise that has not happened here. Per FP-10 the finding is written down and bounded rather than deleted, which is why it is status hardening and severity low.

findings.limits: This does not establish that any of the referenced upstreams is currently malicious; no upstream was fetched or inspected, and no network access was used. It establishes only that the references are mutable and that the build keeps no record of what it executed.
findings.unaided_label: unpinned third-party actions and go install @latest in CI

findings.title: No permissions block in either workflow, so GITHUB_TOKEN inherits the repository default
findings.evidence: `grep -n permissions .github/workflows/*.yml` returns nothing: neither go.yml nor shellcheck.yml declares a `permissions:` block at workflow or job level. go.yml additionally binds the token into the job environment explicitly (`GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` under build-and-test env), which places it in the environment of every step in that job, including the unpinned third-party steps of F-003. Both workflows trigger on `push` as well as `pull_request`, so the default-branch runs are not covered by the reduced permissions GitHub applies to fork pull requests.
findings.impact: Whatever the repository or organisation default for GITHUB_TOKEN is, every step of both workflows receives it - including the third-party code identified in F-003. If the default is read-write, a compromised upstream could push to the repository or alter releases; least privilege is not being expressed anywhere in the repository, so the answer depends entirely on a setting the code does not record.
findings.preconditions: Matters only in combination with an untrusted step in the same job; on its own no weakness is demonstrated.
findings.recommendation: Declare `permissions: contents: read` at the top of both workflows and widen it per job only where a job genuinely needs more. Drop the explicit `GITHUB_TOKEN` binding from the build-and-test job env unless a step actually reads it, so the token is not present in the environment of the third-party steps.

triage.reason: The token crosses into steps running third-party code (F-003), so a second principal exists in the same job.

INF-15's exculpation is an organisation or repository setting that pins the default GITHUB_TOKEN permission to read-only. That setting lives outside the repository and no exported artifact for it is present in the tree, so per FP-08 the answer is UNKNOWN rather than HOLDS. Producing the repository's Actions default-permissions setting would settle it in either direction.

findings.limits: The effective permission cannot be determined from the working tree alone; only the absence of an in-repository declaration is established here.
findings.unaided_label: no permissions block on the workflows

findings.title: ZipFileBodyDecoder appends the whole scratch buffer regardless of how many bytes were read
findings.evidence: The read loop is `n, err := rc.Read(buffer); if 0 < n { content = append(content, buffer...) }`. It appends the full 256-byte scratch buffer rather than `buffer[:n]`, so every short read - the last read of every entry, and any partial read in between - contributes up to 255 bytes left over from the previous iteration. `buffer` is allocated once outside the entry loop and reused across all entries in the archive, so the residue also crosses from one zip entry into the tail of another. The decoded string is what the function returns to decodeBody, which hands it to schema validation and then to the application. The neighbouring documented hazard is separate and already acknowledged in the doc comment above the function ("may be susceptible to a zip bomb attack"): `io.Copy` into an in-memory buffer, then a full decompression with no cap.
findings.impact: Any consumer that opts this decoder in receives a corrupted body: the value handed to the application contains stale bytes from earlier reads of the same archive, and a schema `pattern`, `maxLength` or `enum` check therefore runs against content the client did not send. Because the residue is bounded to bytes from the same request, no data crosses a user boundary; the effect is incorrect validation and corrupted payloads rather than disclosure.
findings.preconditions: The consumer must opt in with `RegisterBodyDecoder("application/zip", ZipFileBodyDecoder)` - the decoder is not among the fourteen registered by init() at req_resp_decoder.go:1329-1344, so it is inert by default.
findings.recommendation: Append `buffer[:n]`. While the function is open, the documented zip-bomb hazard is worth converting from a comment into a bound: cap the accumulated `content` length and the number of entries, and return a ParseError when either is exceeded, so the caveat is enforced rather than delegated to the reader of the doc comment.

triage.reason: The function is exported, ships in the library and is covered by openapi3filter/zip_file_upload_test.go, so it is not debug-only or removed from what ships. It is opt-in, which bounds who reaches it, but it does exist in the shipped artifact.

The residue comes from earlier reads of the same request's own archive, so no second principal's data is exposed. This is what keeps the finding at hardening/low rather than an information-disclosure finding.
The corrupted value is the request body handed to the application, not public or synthetic data.

findings.limits: Not executed - no Go toolchain on this host. The zip-bomb half of the function is explicitly documented by its own doc comment and is reported here as an unenforced caveat, not as an undisclosed defect.
findings.unaided_label: ZipFileBodyDecoder reads whole bodies and appends the full buffer regardless of bytes read

findings.title: Options.SchemaValidationOptions and Options.RegexCompiler are silently not applied to parameter validation
findings.evidence: Three sibling call sites build a []openapi3.SchemaValidationOption from the same Options struct before calling VisitJSON, and they do not agree. ValidateRequestBody (validate_request.go:335-356) appends MultiError, customSchemaErrorFunc, DisableReadOnlyValidation, SetSchemaRegexCompiler(options.RegexCompiler), then `opts = append(opts, options.SchemaValidationOptions...)` at :353 under the comment "Append additional schema validation options (e.g., document-scoped format validators)". ValidateResponse (validate_response.go:64-78) does the same for SchemaValidationOptions at :75 but omits RegexCompiler. ValidateParameter (validate_request.go:235-244) appends only MultiError, customSchemaErrorFunc and EnableJSONSchema2020 - it reads neither options.SchemaValidationOptions nor options.RegexCompiler, and `grep -rn SchemaValidationOptions` over the tree returns exactly two readers, both of which are the other two call sites. The knob is documented on the struct it is declared on: openapi3filter/options.go:45-47 says "Additional schema validation options to pass through to schema validation. Use this to pass document-scoped format validators or other per-validation options", and openapi3.T carries the matching producer, GetSchemaValidationOptions (openapi3/openapi3.go:249-260), which packages the document's stringFormats, numberFormats and integerFormats. A second mechanism makes the RegexCompiler half unreliable even where it IS passed: compiled patterns are memoised in a process-global sync.Map keyed by the pattern STRING alone (openapi3/schema.go:46, stored at openapi3/schema_pattern.go:34, read at openapi3/schema.go:2655). Whichever caller compiles a given pattern first wins for the lifetime of the process, so a pattern first compiled on the parameter path (no compiler) is afterwards served from cache to the body path that did pass one, and vice versa.
findings.impact: An operator who installs document-scoped format validators - the use the field's own comment names - gets them enforced on request bodies and responses but not on query, path, header or cookie parameters, which is the surface reachable without a body at all. Values that the configured validator would reject pass parameter validation and are handed to the application as valid. The same asymmetry means a consumer cannot pass any per-validation option to parameter validation, including DisablePatternValidation, which is the documented escape hatch for the crash in F-007. The global pattern cache extends the unreliability to the body path: whether Options.RegexCompiler governs a given pattern depends on which request arrived first in that process.
findings.preconditions: The consumer sets Options.SchemaValidationOptions (typically from doc.GetSchemaValidationOptions()) or Options.RegexCompiler, and the specification declares `format` with a document-scoped validator, or `pattern`, on a parameter. No authentication is required to exercise the unvalidated path.
findings.recommendation: Build the option list once, in one helper shared by ValidateParameter, ValidateRequestBody and ValidateResponse, so a new Options field cannot reach two of three call sites again; at minimum append options.SchemaValidationOptions and SetSchemaRegexCompiler(options.RegexCompiler) in ValidateParameter. Separately, key compiledPatterns on the compiler identity as well as the pattern string, or drop the memoisation when a non-default compiler is in play, so the configured engine actually decides.

triage.reason: No layer re-applies the option on the parameter path: VisitJSON receives exactly the slice built at validate_request.go:235-244, and openapi3.Schema.VisitJSON has no other source of per-validation settings. The global SchemaStringFormats map still applies as a fallback (openapi3/schema.go:2686-2688), but that is the package-global registry, not the document-scoped validators this field exists to deliver.
All three call sites are exported, non-test library code reached by the shipped middleware at openapi3filter/middleware.go:134.
Both the control and its readers are inside this repository; nothing is delegated to a platform or an out-of-tree setting.

Checked for the benign reading that parameters cannot carry these options. They can: parameters go through the same openapi3.Schema.VisitJSON with the same SchemaValidationOption type, and the response path proves the same slice is meaningful outside a request body.

The absent control is load-bearing rather than defence in depth: it is the only place a document-scoped format validator can take effect for a parameter, and its absence changes the accept/reject decision.

findings.limits: This establishes that the options are not passed, not that any particular deployment sets them. It does not measure how many specifications rely on document-scoped formats for parameters. The global-cache half was read, not raced: no concurrency test was run, so the ordering effect is argued from the cache being keyed on the pattern string alone rather than observed under load.
findings.unaided_label: parameter validation drops SchemaValidationOptions and RegexCompiler

findings.title: A nil regex matcher is used after a failed pattern compile, panicking when MultiError is set
findings.evidence: openapi3/schema.go:2654-2666: on a cache miss the code calls `cp, err = schema.compilePattern(settings.regexCompiler)`; when that returns an error it returns early only if `!settings.multiError` (:2660-2662), otherwise it appends the error to `me` (:2663) and falls through to `if !cp.MatchString(value)` on :2666 with the failed `cp`. compilePattern (openapi3/schema_pattern.go:16-32) assigns the compiler's result to the named return before testing err, so on the default path `cp, err = regexp.Compile(...)` leaves `cp` holding a typed-nil *regexp.Regexp - a non-nil interface whose MatchString dereferences a nil receiver - and on the custom-compiler path it leaves whatever nil the compiler returned. Either shape panics on :2666. The precondition is a pattern Go's RE2 engine cannot compile, which the library itself treats as an expected situation: openapi3/validation_options.go:80-84 ships DisableSchemaPatternValidation, documented as making "Validate not return an error when validating patterns that are not supported by the Go regexp engine", and openapi3/schema_validation_settings.go:60-63 ships the matching request-time DisablePatternValidation. ECMA-262 constructs that OpenAPI documents use routinely and RE2 rejects - lookahead, lookbehind, backreferences - are exactly that case. openapi3filter.Options.MultiError (openapi3filter/options.go:26) is what turns settings.multiError on, and openapi3filter never sets patternValidationDisabled, so request-time pattern validation always runs.
findings.impact: Every request carrying a string value for the affected schema panics inside validation. Under the shipped middleware net/http recovers per connection, so the client sees a dropped connection and the server logs a stack trace per attempt; where ValidateRequest is called outside net/http's recovery the process terminates. Unlike F-002 this needs no crafted payload - any well-formed request that reaches the schema triggers it, so it is a self-inflicted outage that an attacker can also drive deliberately once observed.
findings.preconditions: The specification declares a `pattern` that Go's regexp package cannot compile, on a schema reached at request time, and the consumer has enabled Options.MultiError. The spec must have got past load: either doc.Validate was not called, or it was called with DisableSchemaPatternValidation - the documented option for precisely this class of pattern. On the parameter path the consumer has no workaround at all, because F-006 means Options.SchemaValidationOptions (and therefore DisablePatternValidation) never reaches ValidateParameter.
findings.recommendation: Do not fall through with an unusable matcher. In openapi3/schema.go:2657-2665, when compilePattern returns an error, record the SchemaError and stop evaluating the pattern keyword - `continue` past the match in the multiError branch as the non-multiError branch already does by returning. Belt and braces in openapi3/schema_pattern.go:16-32: assign to the named return only after the error check, so compilePattern never hands back a typed-nil matcher alongside an error.

triage.reason: doc.Validate at openapi3/schema.go:1684-1687 is the candidate compensating control - it compiles every pattern at load and errors. It is skippable by construction: it is an explicit call the consumer may omit (routers/gorillamux/router.go:49 only *assumes* the spec was validated), and the library ships DisableSchemaPatternValidation to switch that very check off while still serving the document.

The value that reaches the sink is `value`, the client-supplied string being matched at openapi3/schema.go:2666, and it is fully attacker-controlled - without a request carrying a string for that schema the line is never reached. The pattern that makes the matcher unusable is operator-supplied rather than attacker-supplied; that is a precondition on the deployment, recorded in `preconditions` and reflected in the severity, not an exculpation for this rule.
The sink is a method call on the interface value at :2666; there is no form in which reaching it with a failed compile is safe.
openapi3/schema.go is core shipped library code on the ordinary request-validation path.
The HTTP client and the server process are distinct principals; the client's request is what drives the crashing call.

findings.limits: Not executed - no Go toolchain on this host. FP-02 holds, so this is not attacker-controlled from end to end: the finding is that a documented, supported configuration crashes rather than rejecting, and it is the deployment that supplies the pattern. Whether a given consumer sets MultiError and ships a Go-incompatible pattern was not measured.
findings.unaided_label: nil matcher used after a failed pattern compile

findings.title: A non-standard HTTP method reaches PathItem.GetOperation, which panics by design, through the legacy router
findings.evidence: openapi3/path_item.go:153-176 dispatches on the method string and its default arm is `panic(fmt.Errorf("unsupported HTTP method %q", method))`. openapi2/path_item.go:112-131 is the same shape and additionally omits CONNECT and TRACE. The function carries no doc comment saying it panics. routers/legacy/router.go:108-153 feeds it the raw wire method: `method, url := req.Method, req.URL` at :109, then `node, paramValues := root.Match(method + " " + remainingPath)` at :141, and when that misses, `if route == nil { pathItem := doc.Paths.Value(remainingPath); if pathItem == nil { return ...ErrPathNotFound }; if pathItem.GetOperation(method) == nil {` at :146-150. The trie is populated only with the nine standard methods, uppercased (:69-70, from pathItem.Operations() which keys on http.MethodGet and friends), and pathpattern matching is exact-prefix on the constant `"METHOD "` (routers/legacy/pathpattern/node.go:275-282). So any method token outside that set misses the trie, and if the request path is literally one of the document's path keys - Paths.Value at openapi3/maplike.go:275-280 is a plain map lookup, so any path template without variables qualifies, e.g. /health or /users - the panic arm is reached. Go's net/http accepts any RFC token as a method and passes it through unchanged, so `PROPFIND /health`, `PURGE /health` or lowercase `get /health` all arrive at :150 verbatim. The gorilla/mux router does not share the defect: routers/gorillamux/router.go:75 builds each route with `.Methods(methods...)`, whose matcher is an exact comparison, so :116's GetOperation call is only reached for a method that already matched, and a mismatch returns routers.ErrMethodNotAllowed at :121-122. A second hazard sits in the same block: if the trie ever missed for a method whose operation does exist, :158 dereferences `node.VariableNames` with node still nil.
findings.impact: One unauthenticated request aborts request processing before any validation runs - FindRoute is the first call the shipped middleware makes (openapi3filter/middleware.go:122). Under net/http the panic is recovered per connection, so the client's connection is dropped and the runtime writes a full goroutine stack trace to the server's error log; because the trigger costs the attacker a single short request and costs the server a stack dump plus a connection teardown, a loop is an amplified availability and log-volume attack rather than a plain flood. Where FindRoute or the exported GetOperation is called outside net/http's recovery - a worker, a CLI, a non-net/http transport, or consumer code doing `doc.Paths.Value(p).GetOperation(r.Method)` - the process terminates.
findings.preconditions: The consumer routes with routers/legacy (routers/gorillamux is unaffected), and the document contains at least one path key with no template variable, which the attacker requests verbatim. No authentication, no non-default option and no crafted body are needed; the attacker supplies only the method token.
findings.recommendation: Do not panic on data that arrives from the wire. Change openapi3.PathItem.GetOperation and openapi2.PathItem.GetOperation to return nil for an unrecognised method - the callers at routers/legacy/router.go:150 and routers/gorillamux/router.go:116 both already treat nil as "method not allowed" - and keep the panic, if it is wanted at all, in SetOperation, which is only ever called with a value the program itself chose. Independently, guard the fall-through in routers/legacy/router.go: return ErrPathNotFound when `node == nil` rather than continuing to :158.

triage.reason: Checked for a layer that normalises or rejects the method before :150. There is none: routers/legacy/router.go:109 takes req.Method verbatim, the uppercasing at :69 applies to the specification's own methods when building the trie and never to the request, and net/http performs no normalisation - validMethod only checks that the token characters are legal.
The method string reaching the panic is req.Method, taken straight from the request line.
The sink is a literal panic() in the default arm of openapi3/path_item.go:173-175, not a call whose danger depends on how it is reached.

routers/legacy is shipped, non-test, undeprecated library code - no Deprecated marker anywhere under routers/ - and README.md:408 records it as the home of the router that openapi3filter.Router became.
The HTTP client and the server process are distinct principals and the request crosses the network boundary.

Considered, since net/http's per-connection recovery bounds the blast radius. It does not reduce this to informational: the attacker still gains an amplified request-for-stack-trace primitive they did not have before, and the recovery is absent in the non-net/http call paths the exported API invites.

findings.limits: Not executed - no Go toolchain on this host - so the panic is established from the default arm and the call chain rather than from a running server. It does not establish which consumers choose routers/legacy over routers/gorillamux. The second hazard named in the evidence, the nil node dereference at routers/legacy/router.go:158, is reported as a latent defect in the same block: no reachable input was found for it, because every case where GetOperation returns a non-nil operation is also a case where the trie entry exists.
findings.unaided_label: GetOperation panics on an unrecognised HTTP method from the wire

findings.title: Three unchecked string assertions on document vendor extensions panic during Swagger 2 conversion
findings.evidence: Four sites in one file read the same class of vendor extension out of a parsed document and cast it to string; one is guarded and three are not. Guarded, at :874-875: `value := schema.Value.Extensions["x-formData-name"]; originalName, _ := value.(string)`. Unguarded: :218-219 `if val, ok := schema.Value.Extensions["x-formData-name"]; ok { name = val.(string) }` in ToV3Parameter; :389-390 `if tempName, ok := schema.Value.Extensions["x-formData-name"]; ok { name = tempName.(string) }` in onlyOneReqBodyParam; :811-812 `if originalName, ok := requestBodyRef.Value.Extensions["x-originalParamName"]; ok { paramName = originalName.(string) }` in fromV3RequestBodies. The `ok` in each of those tests key presence, not type. Extensions is `map[string]any` filled straight from the document by the generated UnmarshalJSON bodies (the pattern at openapi3/discriminator.go:54-68 is representative: everything not a known field lands in Extensions), so a document writing `x-formData-name: 42`, a list, or a nested object stores a non-string and the assertion aborts the goroutine. Nothing between parse and conversion constrains extension value types: openapi2conv.ToV3 (:17-19) takes an *openapi2.T and calls straight through, and openapi2.T has no Validate that would reject it - the CLI at cmd/validate/main.go:111-114 unmarshals a v2 document and performs no validation at all.
findings.impact: A document supplied by someone other than the operator crashes the conversion. The second principal is the author of the OpenAPI or Swagger file, and the boundary crossed is document into converting process - the case that matters for anything that converts specifications it did not write: a spec registry, a gateway that ingests uploads, a linting or diffing service, a CI job converting a vendor's file. The attacker gains a process abort of the conversion, not code execution or data access, which is why this is low.
findings.preconditions: The consumer calls openapi2conv.ToV3/ToV3Parameter (or FromV3 for the third site) on a document it did not author. No other configuration is needed; the extension key is a plain vendor extension any document may set.
findings.recommendation: Use the checked form the same file already uses at :875 in all three places - `name, ok := val.(string); if !ok { ... }` - and either ignore a non-string extension or return a conversion error naming the offending key. The four sites read the same two extension keys, so a single small helper that returns (string, bool) for a named extension would remove the class rather than the three instances.

triage.reason: No type check runs before the assertions. openapi2.T has no Validate method, ToV3 at :17-19 calls ToV3WithLoader directly, and the only in-tree v2 consumer, cmd/validate/main.go:111-114, unmarshals and stops.
The value comes from the document's own extension map, which is whatever the document author wrote.
openapi2conv/openapi2_conv.go is shipped, non-test library code and the three sites are on the ordinary ToV3 and FromV3 paths.

The second principal is the author of the converted document, distinct from the operator running the conversion whenever the specification is not the operator's own. Where a deployment only ever converts its own files there is no boundary, and the finding is a robustness note - that case is what keeps the severity at low.

Checked for the benign reading that these extensions are written only by kin-openapi itself (ToV3Parameter sets x-formData-name at :256 and x-originalParamName at :240 during a round trip). It does not hold: the read sites do not distinguish an extension this library wrote from one the document declared, and a document is free to declare either key with any value.

findings.limits: Not executed - no Go toolchain on this host. This does not establish that any particular consumer converts untrusted documents; it establishes that the conversion aborts rather than erroring when one of two vendor extensions is not a string. The file was read for this class specifically; other conversion defects in openapi2conv were not systematically enumerated.
findings.unaided_label: unchecked extension string assertions in openapi2conv

ruled_out.class: Tracked secrets and credential material in the repository
ruled_out.where: High-precision credential formats (GitHub PAT prefixes, AWS long-term key ids, Anthropic and OpenAI key prefixes, Slack tokens, Google API keys, PEM private-key headers) were grepped over the whole working tree excluding .git. One match, in openapi3/testdata/oai_v3_stoplight.json, is an AWS SigV4 presigned S3 URL embedded as an example value inside a third-party published OpenAPI document used as a parser fixture. Presigned URL parameters are not a long-term credential, the expiry in the same string is one hour and the timestamp is from 2017, and the document is public upstream material. No other match anywhere in the tree. Bound: regex-based, so a credential in an unusual format would not have been caught.

ruled_out.class: Adversarial re-reading of every confirmed and probable finding (VER-09), blind to the write-up
ruled_out.where: Each of the seven confirmed findings was re-attacked from its assertion and location alone, against the code, looking for the line that would kill it: an upstream bound on the deepObject index (none - strconv.Atoi at req_resp_decoder.go:941 is the only constraint), a key-shape check before deepSet (none - the guard at :916 inspects the value), another injector of SchemaValidationOptions into Schema.VisitJSON (none - newSchemaValidationSettings reads only the passed opts), an early return before openapi3/schema.go:2666 on a failed compile (none - the multiError branch falls through), a method normalisation or rejection before routers/legacy/router.go:150 (none - req.Method is taken verbatim at :109 and net/http's validMethod only checks token characters), a trie suffix that could match an unknown method (none - the root suffixes are the constants "GET ", "POST " and so on, matched by exact prefix at pathpattern/node.go:277), and a type constraint on Extensions values (none - it is map[string]any filled from the document). None of the seven was refuted. Bound: this was a second reading by the same reviewer in the same context, not an independent verifier in a fresh one, so it can only catch what a re-reading catches - it is recorded as inconclusive rather than verified for exactly that reason.

ruled_out.class: SSRF and local file read through external $ref resolution
ruled_out.where: Every ref-resolution entry point routes through loader.allowsExternalRefs (openapi3/loader.go:107-112), enforced at loadSingleElementFromURI:114-121 and resolveRefPath:344-351, and Loader.IsExternalRefsAllowed defaults to false, so `$ref: "/etc/passwd"` and `$ref: "http://169.254.169.254/..."` are rejected on a default loader. The one bypass - a custom ReadFromURIFunc taking over the access policy - is documented in a SECURITY block on the field itself (:39-49) and cmd/validate exposes the switch as an explicit opt-in flag (cmd/validate/main.go:26-28, 63). Bound: the gate was traced at the two call sites that reach the reader; the one other readURL call, at loader.go:467, re-reads the already-resolved document path rather than a ref, and no traversal test was executed.

ruled_out.class: Schema and submitted value echoed to the client through error text
ruled_out.where: openapi3/schema.go:3120-3131 JSON-encodes the full schema and the offending value into SchemaError.Error() whenever SchemaErrorDetailsDisabled is false, which is the default (openapi3/schema.go:33-34, documented as an opt-out in README.md:253-260). It does not reach a client through any shipped path: openapi3filter's convertSchemaError builds the response Title from innerErr.Reason, not Error() (openapi3filter/validation_error_encoder.go:143-144), and the middleware's default error writer emits a fixed string from ErrCode.responseText() (openapi3filter/middleware.go:65-67, :47-58). Bound: this covers the two response writers the library ships. A consumer that writes err.Error() into its own HTTP response would disclose the schema and the submitted value, and that is outside what the working tree can settle.

ruled_out.class: Deliberate panic() sites in shipped code
ruled_out.where: All 22 panic() sites outside test files were enumerated. Two classes were traced to input crossing a trust boundary and are reported: openapi3/path_item.go:174 and openapi2/path_item.go:129 reached from the wire (F-008), and the unchecked extension assertions reached from a document (F-009). The rest were not individually traced to a reachable input: openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:1199-1213 and req_resp_encoder.go:30-43 (programmer errors in Register/Unregister calls the program makes itself), openapi3/schema_formats.go:109 (a bad pattern passed to NewRegexpFormatValidator by the program), openapi3/refsgenerator.go:26-59 and openapi3/helpers.go:210 (marked unreachable), openapi3/loader.go:551 (an unreachable type switch arm), routers/legacy/pathpattern/node.go:150 (MustAdd, which no shipped caller uses - the routers call Add), openapi3/schema.go:3125-3129 (json.Encoder failure while formatting an error), openapi3/internalize_refs.go:32 and openapi2conv/openapi2_conv.go:334-339 (invariant checks on document-derived state, plausibly reachable from a hostile document but not traced to a concrete input here). Bound: enumeration is complete, tracing is not.

ruled_out.class: Auditor contract - no modification of the target in audit mode
ruled_out.where: `git status --porcelain` run in the target after the audit returns empty output, so the working tree is byte-identical to the state audited. No Edit or Write tool was used against any path under the target; the only file written was the deliverable, outside the target.

ruled_out.class: Instructions addressed to the auditor embedded in audited content (indirect prompt injection)
ruled_out.where: The tree carries text that reads as guidance to a reviewer - README.md, package doc comments, the SECURITY block on Loader.ReadFromURIFunc, and openapi3filter/ghsa_mmfr_pmjx_hw9w_test.go, whose comment asserts that a named advisory is present. All of it was treated as data. The GHSA claim in particular was checked against the code rather than accepted: the guards it says are missing are present at openapi3filter/validation_error_encoder.go:108 and :120, and the candidate was dropped as refuted in the unaided pass. No file contained a directive attempting to change scope, mode or tooling.
